periods.activity_title: Folding to Find: What Is a Line of Symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.1 p.219
textbook_items_in_class.description: Do you see any line of symmetry in the opening figures (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.1 p.219
textbook_items_in_class.description: For each of five given polygon figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry if any exist.

time_bands.activity: Open with Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1 p.219) ("do you see any line of symmetry in the opening figures...."). Students observe flowers, butterflies, rangoli, and pinwheels and share which figures look the same on both sides, surfacing informal understanding of balance and repetition.

Introduce the folding test: teacher demonstrates folding a triangle along a dotted line so both halves overlap exactly — these halves are called mirror halves — and contrasts this with a four-piece puzzle figure that does not overlap when folded. Students state, in their own words, what a line of symmetry means based on this evidence.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1 p.219) ("for each of five given polygon figures, identify the line(s) of symmetry...."). Each student folds or imagines folding each polygon and records which figures pass the overlap test and where the fold line lies.

Pairs share their answers; class compiles a short list of figures that have a line of symmetry and figures that do not, articulating the formal definition — a line of symmetry cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded along that line.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who mark any vertical line through a figure as a line of symmetry without checking whether folding produces exact overlap — a common error. Encourage students to physically fold or trace-and-flip their drawings rather than relying on visual estimation alone.

periods.activity_title: How Many Folds? Discovering Multiple Lines of Symmetry

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Folding a square — finding all lines of symmetry, section 9.1 p.220
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students take a square piece of paper and fold it four times (vertically, horizontally, along each diagonal) to discover that a square has four lines of symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the diagonal of a rectangle (that is not a square) a line of symmetry? Fold a rectangular piece of paper along its diagonal to check whether the two parts overlap.

time_bands.activity: Students recall that a line of symmetry divides a figure into two mirror halves that overlap exactly. Teacher poses: can a single figure have more than one such line?

Students carry out Activity: Folding a square — finding all lines of symmetry (section 9.1 p.220) ("students take a square piece of paper and fold it four times...."). Each fold — vertical, horizontal, and both diagonals — is tested for exact overlap, and the four fold lines are marked on a sketch.

Students answer Figure it Out (section 9.1 p.221) ("is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap?...."). Pairs discuss whether any further fold could be a line of symmetry and conclude that the square has exactly four.

Students fold a non-square rectangle along its diagonal and work on Figure it Out (section 9.1 p.221) ("is the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square a line of symmetry?...."). They observe that the diagonal fold does not produce overlapping halves and articulate why the rectangle's diagonal fails the symmetry test.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is assuming that any fold that divides a figure in half is a line of symmetry — the diagonal-rectangle investigation directly targets this. After the folding, ask students to explain in words why the overlap fails, linking the result to the formal definition established with the triangle.

periods.activity_title: Reasoning About Multiple Axes of Symmetry

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is the diagonal of a rectangle (that is not a square) a line of symmetry? Fold a rectangular piece of paper along its diagonal to check whether the two parts overlap.

time_bands.activity: Starting from the established definition — a line of symmetry produces exact overlap on folding — the teacher presents several figures: an equilateral triangle, a regular hexagon, and a non-regular quadrilateral. Students predict how many lines of symmetry each figure has and justify their prediction before any folding.

Students revisit Figure it Out (section 9.1 p.221) ("is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap?....") and Figure it Out (section 9.1 p.221) ("is the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square a line of symmetry?...."), now writing a reason — not just an observation — for each answer. For the rectangle, they argue from the mismatch of side lengths.

Small groups examine the labelled square (corners A, B, C, D) discussed in the text: folding along the vertical line of symmetry maps corner B onto A and C onto D. Groups trace what happens to each corner under each of the four folds and record their reasoning — connecting reflection symmetry to the formal idea that each point on one side maps to a matching point on the other.

Class discussion: students share one reasoning chain — e.g., why the rectangle's diagonal cannot be a line of symmetry — and identify the general principle that equal side lengths and equal angle measures are what allow a fold to produce exact overlap.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established through folding that a square has four lines of symmetry and a non-square rectangle has two, students are now reasoning about why rather than just observing what — watch that justifications refer to the fold-and-overlap definition, not to visual appearance. A corner-labelling diagram on the board helps students track where each point moves under reflection.
materials: Square and rectangular paper for reference

periods.activity_title: Ink Blots and Paper Cuts: Making Symmetric Shapes

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Ink Blot Devils, section 9.1 p.222
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students fold paper in half, spill ink on one half, press halves together, and open to observe the symmetric figure formed, identifying the fold as the line of symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Paper Folding and Cutting, section 9.1 p.223
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students fold paper and cut along dotted lines to generate symmetric shapes; a more intricate variant uses multiple folds to create decorative cut-out patterns with identifiable lines of symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the definition of line of symmetry established through folding: if a fold line produces exact overlap, the figure has a line of symmetry at that fold. Today students will use this principle in reverse — deliberately constructing figures that are symmetric.

Students perform Activity: Ink Blot Devils (section 9.1 p.222) ("students fold paper in half, spill ink on one half, press halves together...."). Each student folds a sheet, applies ink or paint, presses, opens, and identifies the fold line as the line of symmetry of the resulting shape.

Students perform Activity: Paper Folding and Cutting (section 9.1 p.223) ("students fold paper and cut along dotted lines to generate symmetric shapes...."). They first try a single fold and one cut, then attempt a multiple-fold variant to produce a decorative pattern. For each result they draw the line(s) of symmetry on the opened sheet.
Each student holds up their cut-out and states aloud how many lines of symmetry it has and where each line lies, using the fold-and-overlap definition to justify their count.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes believe that any decorative cut-out is automatically symmetric — encourage them to check by folding back along the claimed line and testing overlap. Ink blot shapes may appear symmetric but have slight asymmetry at edges; this is a productive discussion point about precision.

periods.activity_title: Punching Holes: Predicting Symmetric Patterns

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Punching Game, section 9.1 p.223
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students punch holes at different locations of a folded square sheet to create symmetric patterns, using the fold as the line of symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.1 p.224
textbook_items_in_class.description: In each of four figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet and then unfolded. Identify the fold line. For figure (d), created by a single punch, determine how the paper was folded.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.1 p.224
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given the line(s) of symmetry, find the location of the other hole(s) in each of five figures.

time_bands.activity: Students perform Activity: Punching Game (section 9.1 p.223) ("students punch holes at different locations of a folded square sheet to create symmetric patterns...."). Each student folds a square sheet once, punches a hole at a chosen location, unfolds, and observes the symmetric pair of holes.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.1 p.224) ("in each of four figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet and then unfolded...."). For each given hole pattern, they identify where the fold line must have been, reasoning from the symmetry of the hole positions.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.1 p.224) ("given the line(s) of symmetry, find the location of the other hole(s)...."). Given a hole and a stated line of symmetry, students locate the mirror-image hole by applying the definition of reflection across that line.
Whole-class check: teacher selects two contrasting cases from Q2 — one with a vertical fold line and one with a diagonal — and students explain how they determined the reflected hole's position.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse reflecting a point across a diagonal line with reflecting across a horizontal or vertical line; the Punching Game makes the error visible immediately when the unfolded sheet is held up. For Q2's diagonal cases, encourage students to fold the paper along the stated line of symmetry and physically mark the hole's mirror position.
materials: A hole punch (or a sharp pencil tip)

periods.activity_title: Predict, Cut, and Check: Paper Shapes and Holes

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 9.1 p.224
textbook_items_in_class.description: Paper cutting questions using vertical and horizontal fold notation; interpret representations of folded paper and associated cuts.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 9.1 p.225
textbook_items_in_class.description: After each of four cuts on folded paper, predict the shape of the hole when the paper is opened; make cutouts to verify predictions — sub-parts (a), (b), (c), (d).

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates reading a folded-paper diagram: vertical fold notation and horizontal fold notation are explained, then a single cut is shown. Students identify what the opened shape will look like before any paper is cut.

Students work on Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.1 p.224) ("paper cutting questions using vertical and horizontal fold notation; interpret representations of folded paper...."). For each diagram, they interpret the fold and cut, then sketch the opened shape.

Students work on Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.1 p.225) ("after each of four cuts on folded paper, predict the shape of the hole when the paper is opened...."). For each sub-part, students first write their prediction, then fold and cut actual paper to verify — recording whether the prediction matched the outcome.
Brief share: one student explains a case where prediction and result differed and identifies the reasoning error, reinforcing the connection between fold direction and the final symmetric shape.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often underestimate how a corner cut on a double-folded sheet produces four identical pieces — emphasise tracking the number of layers before cutting. Encouraging written predictions before cutting develops the habit of reasoning about symmetry before resorting to trial-and-error.

periods.activity_title: Single Cut, Many Shapes: From Folds to Symmetric Holes

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 9.1 p.226
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine how to obtain each of two shapes (both with a square hole in the centre) using folds and a single straight cut — sub-parts (a) aligned-square hole and (b) diamond-orientation square hole.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 9.1 p.226
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry do these shapes have? (a) two figures — a 4-pointed star (square) and an 8-pointed star; (b) a triangle with equal sides and equal angles; (c) a hexagon with equal sides and equal angles.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.1 p.226) ("determine how to obtain each of two shapes — both with a square hole — using folds and a single straight cut...."). For each sub-part, students plan the fold sequence and cut angle in writing, then make the cutout to verify.

Students work on Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.1 p.226) ("how many lines of symmetry do these shapes have?...."). They count lines of symmetry for a 4-pointed star, an 8-pointed star, an equilateral triangle, and a regular hexagon, recording each count with a drawn line.

Class compiles results from Q6 into a shared table: shape name and number of lines of symmetry. Students are prompted to notice whether a pattern connects the number of sides (or points) to the number of symmetry lines for the regular shapes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often struggle with the diamond-orientation hole in Q5(b) because they do not see that a 45° fold before cutting produces the rotated square; prompt them to think about what orientation the fold layers create rather than what the final hole looks like. The table built in the closing band plants the seed for the regular-polygon generalisation developed more fully in section 9.2.

periods.activity_title: Completing and Creating: Symmetry on Grids

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 9.1 p.227
textbook_items_in_class.description: Trace each of eight figures (arrangements of rhombus shapes and polygons on grids) and draw the lines of symmetry, if any.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 9.1 p.228
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the lines of symmetry for the given kolam (traditional Indian dot pattern).

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 9.1 p.228
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw: (a) a triangle with exactly one line of symmetry; (b) a triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry; (c) a triangle with no line of symmetry. Is it possible to draw a triangle with exactly two lines of symmetry?

time_bands.activity: Students trace figures from Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.1 p.227) ("trace each of eight figures — arrangements of rhombus shapes and polygons on grids....") and draw all lines of symmetry. For figures with no line of symmetry, they write a one-sentence reason why no fold produces exact overlap.

Students work on Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.1 p.228) ("find the lines of symmetry for the given kolam...."). They trace the kolam pattern and systematically check candidate fold lines — horizontal, vertical, diagonal — against the overlap definition.

Students work on Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.1 p.228) ("draw: a triangle with exactly one line of symmetry; a triangle with exactly three lines of symmetry; a triangle with no line of symmetry...."). After drawing each, they fold or trace to verify the count. They also address the question of whether exactly two lines are possible.
Quick pair-share: can a triangle have exactly two lines of symmetry? Students exchange reasoning with a partner and the class agrees on an answer.

periods.teacher_notes: The kolam in Q8 often has more lines of symmetry than students initially spot — encourage a systematic check of at least four candidate lines before concluding. The Q9 question about exactly two lines of symmetry in a triangle is a genuine reasoning task: students should argue from the constraint that if two sides are equal a third must follow, not simply draw and check.
materials: Tracing paper or thin plain paper

periods.activity_title: Curved Figures, Completing Halves, and the Symmetry Census

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 9.1 p.228
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw figures containing at least one curved boundary with exactly: (a) one line of symmetry; (b) two lines of symmetry; (c) four lines of symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 9.1 p.228
textbook_items_in_class.description: Copy six partial figures on squared paper and complete each so that the given blue line is a line of symmetry — sub-parts (a) through (f), with a hint to rotate the book for (c) and (f).

time_bands.activity: Students work on Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.1 p.228) ("draw figures containing at least one curved boundary with exactly one, two, or four lines of symmetry...."). For each sub-part they first sketch a candidate, then check by folding or tracing to confirm the exact count of symmetry lines.

Students copy partial figures onto squared paper and work on Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.1 p.228) ("copy six partial figures on squared paper and complete each so that the given blue line is a line of symmetry...."). For each partial figure, they reflect each existing point across the given line to locate the completing points, then join them.

Students inspect their completed figures and count the total lines of symmetry for each — asking whether completing the figure to satisfy one line of symmetry sometimes introduces additional lines as a bonus.

periods.teacher_notes: When completing partial figures on squared paper, students often reflect horizontally or vertically but make errors with diagonal symmetry lines — for sub-parts (c) and (f), prompt them to rotate the page as the textbook suggests. In Q10, a common error is drawing a figure with more symmetry lines than required; encourage students to actively break extra symmetry.

periods.activity_title: Two-Line Symmetry and Dot-Grid Extensions

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 9.1 p.229
textbook_items_in_class.description: Copy six partial drawings on squared paper and complete each so that the resulting figure has both blue lines as lines of symmetry — sub-parts (a) through (f).

textbook_items_in_class.source_section: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 9.1 p.230
textbook_items_in_class.description: Copy six figures on a dot grid and for each draw two more line segments to make a shape that has a line of symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Students copy partial drawings and work on Figure it Out Q12 (section 9.1 p.229) ("copy six partial drawings on squared paper and complete each so that the resulting figure has both blue lines as lines of symmetry...."). For each figure, they must satisfy two symmetry lines simultaneously — reflecting across the first line, then checking that the result also satisfies the second.

Students copy dot-grid figures and work on Figure it Out Q13 (section 9.1 p.230) ("copy six figures on a dot grid and for each draw two more line segments to make a shape that has a line of symmetry...."). For each given partial figure, students choose two segments that complete it symmetrically and draw the resulting line of symmetry.
Students select one Q13 figure and explain to a partner how they chose the two added segments and where the line of symmetry lies, using the fold-and-overlap definition as the justification.

periods.teacher_notes: In Q12, satisfying two simultaneous lines of symmetry is significantly harder than one — students may complete the first reflection correctly but then find the second line violated; encourage them to check both lines after every addition rather than completing the whole figure and checking at the end. The dot grid in Q13 helpfully constrains candidate segments; watch that students are adding exactly two segments, not more.

periods.activity_title: The Windmill Spins: Introducing Rotational Symmetry

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.2 p.235
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the angles of symmetry for three given figures about the marked centre point — sub-parts (a), (b), (c).

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the paper windmill — a figure with no line of symmetry — and rotates a cutout or diagram by 90° about its centre, showing that the figure looks exactly the same. The terms centre of rotation, angle of rotational symmetry, and angle of symmetry are introduced. Students note that 90°, 180°, 270°, and 360° all return the windmill to an identical appearance.

Teacher demonstrates a labelled square, tracking corner positions after each 90° rotation to show that the square also has four angles of symmetry. Students observe how labelling corners reveals what changes even when the overall figure looks unchanged.

Students begin Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2 p.235) ("find the angles of symmetry for three given figures about the marked centre point...."). For each figure they trace the shape, rotate the tracing, and record each angle at which the tracing matches the original — listing all angles of symmetry.
Students state the definition of angle of rotational symmetry in their own words and confirm that 360° is always included in the list for any figure.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume that a figure with rotational symmetry must also have reflection symmetry — the windmill is the canonical counterexample, and it is worth dwelling on it before moving to the square. Watch for students listing only the smallest angle of symmetry; prompt them to find all angles by continuing to rotate past the first match.

periods.activity_title: Listing Angles: Which Figures Rotate Into Themselves?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.235
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of seven given figures have more than one angle of symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 9.2 p.236
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give the order of rotational symmetry for each of six figures (including an arrow, X-shape, star, tumbling figure, plus-shape, and pentagon).

time_bands.activity: Building on the established definition — an angle of symmetry is any angle through which the figure looks exactly the same — teacher introduces the order of rotational symmetry: the count of distinct angles of symmetry a figure has (including 360°).

Students work on Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2 p.235) ("which of seven given figures have more than one angle of symmetry?...."). For each figure they use tracing paper to test multiple rotation angles and classify the figure as having exactly one angle (360° only) or more.

Students work on Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2 p.236) ("give the order of rotational symmetry for each of six figures...."). For each figure — arrow, X-shape, star, tumbling figure, plus-shape, pentagon — they list all angles of symmetry and count them to state the order.
Class discussion: students compare orders across the six figures and articulate a pattern — a figure with order n has angles that are multiples of 360°/n.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes include angles beyond 360° in their list — reinforce that the range is 0° (exclusive) to 360° (inclusive). The arrow and tumbling figure in Q3 are often incorrectly given order 2; trace-and-rotate verification resolves this.

periods.activity_title: Radial Arms and the 360°/n Rule

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example, section 9.2 p.232
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the angles of symmetry of a parallelogram-strip shape. A 180° rotation is demonstrated not to overlap with the original (asymmetry of the parallelogram); the figure returns to itself only after 360°, so it does not have rotational symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Paper cutout rotation — three-arm radial figure, section 9.2 p.233
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students trace and cut out a three-arm radial figure, then rotate the cutout over the original figure to determine its angles of rotation and verify observations about rotational symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Class reads and discusses Example (section 9.2 p.232) ("find the angles of symmetry of a parallelogram-strip shape...."). Students follow the reasoning that a 180° rotation produces a differently oriented parallelogram — not an identical image — and that only 360° works, so the figure lacks rotational symmetry.

Students perform Activity: Paper cutout rotation — three-arm radial figure (section 9.2 p.233) ("students trace and cut out a three-arm radial figure, then rotate the cutout over the original figure...."). For arms spaced 120° apart, students discover angles of symmetry 120°, 240°, 360° and confirm the pattern.

Students examine radial figures with 4 arms (90° spacing) and 5 arms (72° spacing), listing angles of symmetry in each case. They then attempt to generalise: for n equal radial arms, the smallest angle of symmetry is 360°/n and all angles of symmetry are multiples of this value.
Students write the generalisation in their own words and test it on the windmill (4 arms, 90° spacing) as a verification — does 360°/4 = 90° match what they found in the earlier exploration?

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored the parallelogram's lack of rotational symmetry alongside figures that do have it, students are now ready to generalise — watch that they state the 360°/n rule as applying only to figures with n equally spaced radial arms, not to all n-sided figures. The verification against the windmill is important: students should be able to confirm the formula rather than just memorise it.

periods.activity_title: True or False: Reasoning About Angles of Symmetry

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.2 p.235
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the angles of symmetry for three given figures about the marked centre point — sub-parts (a), (b), (c).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.235
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which of seven given figures have more than one angle of symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 9.2 p.236
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give the order of rotational symmetry for each of six figures (including an arrow, X-shape, star, tumbling figure, plus-shape, and pentagon).

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses two True/False statements from the section: (1) 360° is always an angle of symmetry for any figure; (2) the smallest whole-number angle of symmetry of a figure must be a factor of 360. Students vote silently, then prepare a written justification.

Students present their justifications in pairs, using the 360°/n generalisation as their deductive chain. Teacher highlights correct proofs and identifies gaps — e.g., students who argue from examples only rather than from the general rule.

Students revisit Figure it Out Q1–Q3 (section 9.2 p.235–236) to apply the deductive chain: for each figure with known order, they verify that every stated angle of symmetry is indeed a multiple of the smallest, and that the smallest is a factor of 360.

Students consider the case of 7 equal radial arms: 360°/7 ≈ 51 3/7°, not a whole number. They reason about why no whole-number angle of symmetry exists for 7 arms and what this reveals about the factor condition.

periods.teacher_notes: The factor-of-360 condition is the key deductive result of section 9.2 and students often state it correctly for integer cases without seeing why non-integer smallest angles fail — the 7-arm case makes the reasoning concrete. Encourage students to argue from the generalisation, not from individual figures.

periods.activity_title: The Circle: Every Angle, Every Diameter

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Colour the sectors of a 12-sector circle so that the figure has (i) 3 angles of symmetry, (ii) 4 angles of symmetry; (iii) determine all possible numbers of angles of symmetry obtainable by colouring sectors.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the circle's unique properties: every rotation about the centre returns the circle to itself, so every angle is an angle of symmetry; and every diameter is a line of reflection symmetry. Real-world examples — ceiling fans at different speeds, a wheel, a flower with many petals — illustrate these properties. Students state the two key facts in their own words.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1 (section 9.2 p.238) ("colour the sectors of a 12-sector circle so that the figure has 3 angles of symmetry, 4 angles of symmetry; determine all possible numbers...."). For parts (i) and (ii), they plan a colouring that achieves the required angles, using the 360°/n rule. For part (iii), they list which divisors of 12 are achievable.
Students share their colouring strategies for Q1(iii) — which divisors of 12 yield valid colourings and which do not — and explain why the 12-sector constraint limits achievable symmetry counts.

Students compare the circle (infinitely many angles of symmetry, infinitely many lines of symmetry) to the regular polygon results they have seen, articulating why the circle is the most symmetric planar figure.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may initially assume that any colouring of 12 sectors can produce any desired number of angles of symmetry — Q1(iii) productively challenges this by requiring them to identify which divisors of 12 are achievable. Watch for the common error of confusing the number of sectors with the number of angles of symmetry.

periods.activity_title: Both Symmetries Together: Drawing Figures That Have Them

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw two figures (other than a circle and a square) that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw rough sketches of: (a) a triangle with ≥2 lines and ≥2 angles of symmetry; (b) a triangle with exactly 1 line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry; (c) a quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry; (d) a quadrilateral with reflection symmetry but no rotational symmetry.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly reviews the two symmetry types defined in the chapter — reflection symmetry (line of symmetry, fold-and-overlap) and rotational symmetry (angle of symmetry, rotate-and-match) — and notes that a figure can possess one, both, or neither.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2 (section 9.2 p.238) ("draw two figures — other than a circle and a square — that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry...."). They sketch candidates, then verify each for both types before committing.

Students work on Figure it Out Q3 (section 9.2 p.238) ("draw rough sketches of: a triangle with ≥2 lines and ≥2 angles of symmetry; a triangle with exactly 1 line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry; a quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry; a quadrilateral with reflection symmetry but no rotational symmetry...."). For each sub-part they check their sketch against both symmetry definitions.
Students share one surprising result — e.g., that a rhombus has reflection symmetry but not rotational symmetry (beyond 180°) — and explain it using the definitions.

periods.teacher_notes: Q3(c) — a quadrilateral with rotational but no reflection symmetry — is the hardest sub-part; students should think of a parallelogram (order-2 rotation, no reflection line). Q3(b) targets the isosceles triangle and Q3(d) a kite or isosceles trapezium — if students draw a triangle for Q3(d), redirect them to the quadrilateral constraint.

periods.activity_title: Reasoning with the Smallest Angle: Factor Problems

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry and the figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can a figure have rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: (a) 45°? (b) 17°?

time_bands.activity: Students apply the deductive chain from the 360°/n generalisation to Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.2 p.238) ("in a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry — what are the other angles...."). They list all multiples of 60° up to and including 360°: 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°, 360°.

Students work on Figure it Out Q5 (section 9.2 p.238) ("in a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry and the figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°...."). They reason: if two angles smaller than 60° exist, 60° must be a multiple of the smallest, narrowing the smallest to 20° or 30°; they determine which value is consistent with 60° being in the list.

Students work on Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.2 p.238) ("can a figure have rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is 45°? 17°?...."). They apply the factor-of-360 condition: 45 divides 360 exactly (360/45 = 8), so yes; 17 does not divide 360 exactly, so no.

Students write a general test sentence: a whole-number angle θ can be the smallest angle of rotational symmetry if and only if 360 is divisible by θ. They verify with one further example of their own choosing.

periods.teacher_notes: Q5 is the most demanding of the three: students must work backward from a known angle to constrain the smallest — watch for students who guess 20° without checking that both 20° and 40° are then angles of symmetry (two values less than 60°). The factor-of-360 test in Q6 should be stated as a criterion, not merely checked case by case.

periods.activity_title: Parliament Building and Real-World Symmetry

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: Parliament Building in Delhi: (a) Does its outer boundary have reflection symmetry — how many lines? (b) Does it have rotational symmetry about its centre — find the angles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity: Playing with Tiles, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students use colour tiles to complete a figure with exactly 2 lines of symmetry, then use 16 tiles to create figures with exactly 1 or 2 lines of symmetry, and make creative symmetric designs.

time_bands.activity: Students examine the Parliament Building diagram and work on Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.2 p.239) ("Parliament Building in Delhi: does its outer boundary have reflection symmetry — how many lines? Does it have rotational symmetry — find the angles?...."). They identify the circular outer boundary's symmetry lines (as diameters) and determine angles of rotational symmetry.

Students perform Activity: Playing with Tiles (section 9.2 p.239) ("students use colour tiles to complete a figure with exactly 2 lines of symmetry, then use 16 tiles to create figures with exactly 1 or 2 lines of symmetry...."). They first complete a given partial tile arrangement, then use 16 tiles freely to produce at least one figure with exactly 1 line of symmetry and one with exactly 2 lines.
Students display their two tile figures and state — for each — where the line(s) of symmetry lie and whether any rotational symmetry is also present.

periods.teacher_notes: The Parliament Building's circular outer boundary has infinitely many lines of symmetry and infinitely many angles of rotational symmetry — students should state this clearly rather than listing a few. In the tiles activity, watch that students count lines of symmetry by testing fold directions across the tile arrangement, not by visual impression.
materials: Colour tiles or coloured square cut-outs (16 per student)

periods.activity_title: Regular Polygons: Counting Lines and Angles of Symmetry

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry do the Regular Polygons (from Chapter 1, Table 3) have? What number sequence do you get?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many angles of symmetry do the Regular Polygons (from Chapter 1, Table 3) have? What number sequence do you get?

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up a systematic investigation: students will work through the regular polygons in order of increasing sides and record their symmetry counts in a table. The two questions to answer for each polygon are: how many lines of symmetry? and how many angles of rotational symmetry?

Students work on Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.2 p.239) ("how many lines of symmetry do the regular polygons have? What number sequence do you get?...."). They draw or trace each regular polygon, mark all lines of symmetry, and record the count in a growing table.

Students work on Figure it Out Q9 (section 9.2 p.239) ("how many angles of symmetry do the regular polygons have? What number sequence do you get?...."). For each polygon, they apply the 360°/n formula to list all angles and count them, adding this column to their table.

Students read across both columns of the table and state what they notice: for a regular n-gon, the number of lines of symmetry equals the number of angles of rotational symmetry equals n, producing the sequence 3, 4, 5, 6, …

periods.teacher_notes: Students often count lines of symmetry correctly for triangles and squares but miscount for pentagons and hexagons — for these, it helps to distinguish lines through vertices from lines through edge midpoints. The matching of line-count and angle-count in both columns is the key inductive result; ensure students write it as a general statement, not just as a table.
materials: Textbook open to section 9.2 p.239 and Chapter 1 Table 3

periods.activity_title: Koch Snowflake and the Ashoka Chakra: Symmetry in Special Figures

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry do the shapes in the Koch Snowflake sequence (Chapter 1, Table 3) have?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does the Ashoka Chakra have?

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly shows the Koch Snowflake sequence from Chapter 1 Table 3 and the Ashoka Chakra, asking students to predict — before analysing — how many lines of symmetry and angles of rotational symmetry each has, noting their predictions.

Students work on Figure it Out Q10 (section 9.2 p.239) ("how many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry do the shapes in the Koch Snowflake sequence have?...."). They examine the initial equilateral triangle and successive iterations, arguing that each stage inherits the triangle's 3-fold symmetry: 3 lines and 3 angles (120°, 240°, 360°).

Students work on Figure it Out Q11 (section 9.2 p.239) ("how many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does the Ashoka Chakra have?...."). They count the spokes (24), apply 360°/24 = 15° as the smallest angle, list all 24 angles of symmetry, and identify the 24 lines of symmetry through the spoke tips.

Students compare predictions with actual results for both figures, noting which predictions were accurate and which required correction, and stating what feature of each figure determines its symmetry counts.

periods.teacher_notes: The Koch Snowflake is visually complex but each iteration preserves the equilateral triangle's 3-fold symmetry — students who count from the figure's edges rather than reasoning from its construction will struggle; prompt them to count radial arms or the order of the underlying triangle. For the Ashoka Chakra, students may miscount spokes; encourage them to count carefully from the image.
materials: Textbook open to section 9.2 p.239 and Chapter 1 Table 3
Coloured pencils (optional, for marking symmetry lines)

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.238

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw rough sketches of: (a) a triangle with ≥2 lines and ≥2 angles of symmetry; (b) a triangle with exactly 1 line of symmetry and no rotational symmetry; (c) a quadrilateral with rotational symmetry but no reflection symmetry; (d) a quadrilateral with reflection symmetry but no rotational symmetry.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: In a figure, 60° is an angle of symmetry and the figure has two angles of symmetry less than 60°. What is its smallest angle of symmetry?

time_bands.activity: Students revisit Figure it Out Q2 and Q3 (section 9.2 p.238) with fresh attention to figures they found difficult in an earlier sitting — for Q3, they focus particularly on the quadrilateral sub-parts, checking each figure against both symmetry definitions and correcting any earlier errors.

Students revisit Figure it Out Q4 (section 9.2 p.238) and Q5 (section 9.2 p.238), verifying their earlier answers by an alternate route: for Q4, multiply 60° by each integer from 1 to 6; for Q5, find all factors of 60° that are also factors of 360° and select the one consistent with exactly two values below 60°.

Students pair up and each poses a new angle-of-symmetry problem of the Q4/Q5 type for their partner: they choose a smallest angle (a factor of 360), state it, and ask the partner to list all angles of symmetry. Partners verify each other's answers.

Class shares one student-posed problem; teacher uses it to confirm the factor-of-360 criterion and the listing rule as the unified framework for both reflection and rotational symmetry in the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates the full span of section 9.2's Symmetries of a Circle content, so it is important that students can articulate both symmetry types clearly before the final synthesis. The partner-posing activity reveals whether students have genuinely internalised the factor-of-360 criterion or are applying it mechanically.

periods.activity_title: Consolidating Rotational Symmetry: From Figures to Generalisations

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 9.2 p.238
textbook_items_in_class.description: Can a figure have rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: (a) 45°? (b) 17°?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: Parliament Building in Delhi: (a) Does its outer boundary have reflection symmetry — how many lines? (b) Does it have rotational symmetry about its centre — find the angles.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 9.2 p.239
textbook_items_in_class.description: How many lines of symmetry do the Regular Polygons (from Chapter 1, Table 3) have? What number sequence do you get?

time_bands.activity: Students revisit Figure it Out Q6 (section 9.2 p.238) ("can a figure have rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is 45°? 17°?...."), now writing a full written justification for each answer using the factor-of-360 criterion rather than a simple yes/no.

Students revisit Figure it Out Q7 (section 9.2 p.239) ("Parliament Building in Delhi: does its outer boundary have reflection symmetry? Does it have rotational symmetry?....") and Figure it Out Q8 (section 9.2 p.239) ("how many lines of symmetry do the regular polygons have?...."), connecting the Parliament Building's circular boundary to the general result that a circle has infinitely many of each.

Students create a personal summary table: for each figure type studied in the chapter (equilateral triangle, square, non-square rectangle, regular pentagon, regular hexagon, circle, parallelogram, windmill, Ashoka Chakra), they record the number of lines of symmetry and the number of angles of rotational symmetry.

Students identify the one figure in their table that has rotational but no reflection symmetry (the windmill / parallelogram) and explain why this is possible — closing the chapter's central contrast between the two symmetry types.

periods.teacher_notes: The personal summary table is a consolidation tool for this unit alone — it begins and ends within these minutes. Students should leave this unit with a clear sense of which figures have only one type of symmetry, both types, or neither, grounded in the definitions.

textbook_items_in_class.description: How many angles of symmetry do the Regular Polygons (from Chapter 1, Table 3) have? What number sequence do you get?

periods.activity_title: Four Problems, Two Symmetries: Putting the Chapter to Work
periods.teacher_notes: Pose all four problems at once on the board. Students work individually with full written working, then compare in groups of three — any disagreement is reconstructed step by step, not settled by majority. Each group nominates one presenter per problem; the presenter states the answer and the class names aloud the chapter method it rested on before the next problem is taken up. Problem 1 needs the fold-and-overlap definition of line of symmetry; watch for students who accept a line that divides area equally without checking exact overlap. Problem 2 needs the reflection-of-a-point rule; the common error is reflecting across the wrong axis. Problem 3 needs the 360°/n rule for radial arms; students sometimes list only the smallest angle and omit the others. Problem 4 needs the factor-of-360 test; students may accept 20° without checking, or reject it by miscounting.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | A figure is folded along a vertical line through its centre. The left half lands exactly on the right half. Then the same figure is folded along a horizontal line through its centre. The left half does NOT land on the right half. How many lines of symmetry does the figure have? Name the type of symmetry it has. | The vertical fold produces exact overlap, so the vertical line is a line of symmetry. The horizontal fold does not produce exact overlap, so the horizontal line is not a line of symmetry. The figure has exactly 1 line of symmetry and possesses reflection symmetry.
2 | A square has corners labelled A (top-left), B (top-right), C (bottom-right), D (bottom-left). It is folded along its vertical line of symmetry (the line midway between the left and right sides). Which corner does B move to, and which corner does C move to? | Folding along the vertical centre line reflects the right side onto the left side. B (top-right) moves to the position of A (top-left). C (bottom-right) moves to the position of D (bottom-left). This uses the rule that reflection maps each point to the point directly opposite it across the fold line at the same perpendicular distance.
3 | A radial figure has 6 arms of equal length, spaced equally around a centre point. List all its angles of rotational symmetry. | Equal spacing means each arm is 360° ÷ 6 = 60° from the next. The figure looks exactly the same after any multiple of 60°. Angles of symmetry: 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°, 360°. There are 6 angles in all.
4 | A student claims that a figure has rotational symmetry with smallest angle of symmetry equal to 20°. Is this possible? Give a reason. Then list all the angles of symmetry such a figure would have. | Test: 360° ÷ 20° = 18, which is a whole number, so 20° is a valid smallest angle (it is a factor of 360). Yes, the claim is possible. All angles of symmetry are multiples of 20° up to 360°: 20°, 40°, 60°, 80°, 100°, 120°, 140°, 160°, 180°, 200°, 220°, 240°, 260°, 280°, 300°, 320°, 340°, 360° — 18 angles in all.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes all four problems on the board, reading each aloud. Students are told they will work alone first, with full written working, and that later each group will reconstruct any disagreement step by step. No discussion yet.

Students work individually on all four problems, writing out every step. Teacher circulates without giving answers — if a student is stuck, ask: 'What does the chapter say about fold-and-overlap?' or 'What is the formula for equally spaced arms?' No hints beyond pointing back to the method.

Groups of three compare answers. Any disagreement is resolved by reconstructing the solution step by step — the group traces where the two workings first differ and identifies which step is in error. Each group nominates one presenter per problem.

Presenters take the board in turn, one problem each. After each answer is stated, the class names aloud the chapter method the solution used — fold-and-overlap definition, reflection of a point across a line, the 360°/n rule for radial arms, or the factor-of-360 test. Teacher confirms or corrects the named method before moving to the next problem.

Teacher states the chapter's one idea: a figure has symmetry when a transformation — a fold or a rotation — leaves it looking exactly the same, and every result in this chapter followed from that single test.

items.prompt: A line of symmetry divides a figure into two parts. Which of the following best describes what must be true of those two parts?

options.label: B
options.text: They must be equal in area but need not have the same shape.

options.label: C
options.text: They must be mirror images but need not overlap when folded.

options.label: D
options.text: They must overlap exactly when the figure is folded along that line.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: They must overlap exactly when the figure is folded along that line.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the fold-and-overlap definition: a line of symmetry is a line along which the figure can be folded so that both halves coincide exactly.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student conflates equal area with symmetry, not recognising that shape and orientation must also match.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student partially understands reflection but misses that the overlap test — not just visual mirror-image appearance — is the defining criterion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student over-restricts the definition to triangular figures, confusing a specific example with the general rule.

inclusivity.support: Let the student fold a square and a non-square rectangle along different lines to see which folds produce exact overlap.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to give one example of two equal-area shapes that are mirror images but whose fold does not produce exact overlap.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.1 p.219
exercise.description: Do you see any line of symmetry in the opening figures (flower, butterfly, rangoli, pinwheel)? What about the picture of the cloud?
