items.section_title: Figures with more than one line of symmetry
items.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4. A square has four lines of symmetry: the vertical midline, the horizontal midline, and the two diagonals.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fold the square along each candidate line (vertical, horizontal, both diagonals) and confirm all four produce exact overlap.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recognises only the most obvious vertical fold line and does not test other directions.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student finds the two midlines (vertical and horizontal) but overlooks the diagonal folds.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student over-counts, perhaps confusing the number of sides with the number of symmetry lines or including half-lines.

inclusivity.support: Have the student physically fold a square piece of paper in four ways and check which folds make the halves overlap.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain in their own words why a non-square rectangle has only 2 lines of symmetry and not 4.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
exercise.description: Is there any other way to fold the square so that the two halves overlap? How many lines of symmetry does the square shape have?

items.prompt: A figure is rotated about a fixed centre point. At which rotation is it guaranteed that the figure will look exactly the same as the original, regardless of what shape the figure is?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 360°. A complete rotation always returns every point to its original position, so 360° is an angle of symmetry for every figure.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition: 360° is always an angle of rotational symmetry because a full rotation returns the figure to its exact original position.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is thinking of the windmill's smallest angle of symmetry and generalising incorrectly to all figures.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be thinking of the parallelogram or a figure with order-2 symmetry, treating a common case as a universal rule.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has guessed a rotation that works for some figures but is not guaranteed for all.

inclusivity.support: Have the student rotate a tracing of a non-symmetric shape (e.g., the letter F) and ask at which angle it first looks the same.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to name two figures whose smallest angle of symmetry is not 360° and state what those smallest angles are.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.2 p.235
exercise.description: Find the angles of symmetry for three given figures about the marked centre point — sub-parts (a), (b), (c).

items.prompt: A windmill shape looks exactly the same after rotations of 90°, 180°, 270°, and 360° about its centre. What is the order of rotational symmetry of the windmill?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4. The windmill has four angles of symmetry (90°, 180°, 270°, 360°), so its order of rotational symmetry is 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the number of distinct angles of symmetry in the given list; the order equals that count.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks a figure with rotational symmetry other than only 360° still has order 1, confusing order with the smallest angle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be counting only 180° and 360° as angles of symmetry, missing the 90° and 270° values.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the smallest angle of symmetry (90°) with the order of rotational symmetry.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to list all angles at which the windmill looks the same and then count the list entries.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student what the order of rotational symmetry of a regular hexagon is and how the 360°/n formula gives this directly.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.235
exercise.description: Which of seven given figures have more than one angle of symmetry?

items.prompt: A circle is rotated about its centre. For which of the following rotation angles does the circle NOT look exactly the same as it did before the rotation?

options.label: D
options.text: The circle looks the same after every rotation about its centre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The circle looks exactly the same after every rotation about its centre — every angle is an angle of symmetry for the circle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the property established in section 9.2: the circle has every angle as an angle of rotational symmetry because rotating it by any amount about the centre maps it onto itself.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not recognise that 30° is also an angle of symmetry; they may think only familiar angles apply.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student does not recognise that 45° is also an angle of symmetry; they may think only divisors of 90° apply.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not recognise that 137° is also an angle of symmetry; they may believe only 'round' angles work.

inclusivity.support: Have the student trace a circle onto paper, rotate the tracing by any angle, and place it back over the original to see it matches every time.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain why no other closed curve — other than the circle — has this property of every angle being an angle of symmetry.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.2 p.238
exercise.description: Colour the sectors of a 12-sector circle so that the figure has (i) 3 angles of symmetry, (ii) 4 angles of symmetry; (iii) determine all possible numbers of angles of symmetry obtainable by colouring sectors.

items.prompt: Which of the following statements about a circle is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: A circle has exactly 2 lines of symmetry.

options.label: B
options.text: A circle has exactly 4 lines of symmetry.

options.label: C
options.text: A circle has no rotational symmetry.

options.label: D
options.text: Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Every diameter of a circle is a line of symmetry. Since there are infinitely many diameters, the circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the symmetry properties of the circle: folding along any diameter produces two semicircles that overlap exactly.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is likely mapping a non-square rectangle's properties onto the circle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be mapping the square's four lines of symmetry onto the circle.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student incorrectly denies the circle's rotational symmetry, perhaps because 'every angle' seems too many to count.

inclusivity.support: Have the student fold a circular paper cut-out along several different diameters and observe that each fold produces exact overlap.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain why the circle's line-of-symmetry count and angle-of-symmetry count are both described as infinite.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 9.2 p.238
exercise.description: Draw two figures (other than a circle and a square) that have both reflection symmetry and rotational symmetry.

items.prompt: A figure has 60° as its smallest angle of rotational symmetry. List all its angles of rotational symmetry up to and including 360°.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The angles of rotational symmetry are 60°, 120°, 180°, 240°, 300°, and 360°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: All angles of symmetry are multiples of the smallest angle of symmetry; list 60° × 1, 60° × 2, … up to 60° × 6 = 360°.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at how multiples of the smallest angle were listed for the windmill and the equilateral triangle in the chapter.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state how many angles of symmetry a figure has if its smallest angle is 60°, then generalise the count for any smallest angle that divides 360°.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 9.2 p.238
exercise.description: In a figure, 60° is the smallest angle of symmetry. What are the other angles of symmetry?

items.prompt: The outer boundary of a building has the shape of a circle. Which of the following is true about its lines of symmetry?

options.label: A
options.text: It has exactly 3 lines of symmetry.

options.label: B
options.text: It has exactly 8 lines of symmetry.

options.label: C
options.text: It has infinitely many lines of symmetry, each passing through the centre.

options.label: D
options.text: It has no lines of symmetry because a building boundary is not a mathematical circle.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: It has infinitely many lines of symmetry, each passing through the centre — every diameter of the circle is a line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the property of the circle: every diameter is a line of reflection symmetry, and since there are infinitely many diameters, there are infinitely many lines of symmetry.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of the equilateral triangle's 3 lines and misapplying it to a circular shape.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be thinking of the octagon's 8 lines and misapplying it to a circular shape.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the idealised mathematical shape with its real-world approximation; the question asks about the circular boundary as a mathematical figure.

inclusivity.support: Have the student draw a circle and fold it along three different diameters, confirming each produces overlap — then ask whether any diameter fails.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to connect the Parliament Building's circular boundary result to the general statement about all circles.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 9.2 p.239
exercise.description: Parliament Building in Delhi: (a) Does its outer boundary have reflection symmetry — how many lines? (b) Does it have rotational symmetry about its centre — find the angles.

items.prompt: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and 5 equal angles. How many lines of symmetry does it have, and how many angles of rotational symmetry does it have? State both answers and explain briefly how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A regular pentagon has 5 lines of symmetry and 5 angles of rotational symmetry (72°, 144°, 216°, 288°, and 360°). For a regular n-gon, the number of lines of symmetry equals n, and the angles of symmetry are multiples of 360°/n — here 360°/5 = 72°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the regular-polygon rule: a regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry and n angles of rotational symmetry, the smallest being 360°/n.

inclusivity.support: Have the student look at the table of regular-polygon results built for Q8 and Q9 and read off the row for n = 5.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to extend their answer: how many lines and angles of symmetry does a regular 12-gon have, and what is its smallest angle of symmetry?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 9.2 p.239
exercise.description: How many lines of symmetry do the Regular Polygons (from Chapter 1, Table 3) have? What number sequence do you get?

items.prompt: An equilateral triangle is the starting shape of the Koch Snowflake sequence. How many angles of rotational symmetry does the equilateral triangle have, and does each iteration of the Koch Snowflake preserve this number?

options.label: A
options.text: The equilateral triangle has 3 angles of symmetry; each Koch iteration also has 3.

options.label: B
options.text: The equilateral triangle has 3 angles of symmetry; later Koch iterations lose this symmetry.

options.label: C
options.text: The equilateral triangle has 4 angles of symmetry because it is a type of star.

options.label: D
options.text: The equilateral triangle has 6 angles of symmetry; Koch iterations reduce this to 3.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The equilateral triangle has 3 angles of rotational symmetry (120°, 240°, 360°), and every iteration of the Koch Snowflake sequence also has exactly 3 — because each iteration adds bumps symmetrically on every edge, preserving the 3-fold symmetry of the original triangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the 360°/n formula for the equilateral triangle (n = 3, smallest angle = 120°) and reason that symmetric edge modifications preserve the underlying symmetry order.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student incorrectly assumes that adding geometric complexity necessarily reduces symmetry.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the number of lines of symmetry with the number of angles of symmetry, double-counting.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student misidentifies the equilateral triangle as a star shape and applies incorrect reasoning.

inclusivity.support: Have the student rotate a tracing of the Koch Snowflake's second iteration by 120° and 240° to observe that it matches the original each time.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain why the symmetry count does not change even as infinitely many bumps are added in later Koch iterations.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 9.2 p.239
exercise.description: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry do the shapes in the Koch Snowflake sequence (Chapter 1, Table 3) have?

items.prompt: The Ashoka Chakra has 24 equally spaced spokes radiating from the centre. What is the smallest angle of rotational symmetry of the Ashoka Chakra? How many angles of rotational symmetry does it have in total?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The smallest angle of rotational symmetry is 360° ÷ 24 = 15°. The total number of angles of rotational symmetry is 24 (the multiples of 15° from 15° up to 360°).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the 360°/n formula with n = 24 to find the smallest angle, then count all multiples of that angle up to 360°.

inclusivity.support: Have the student use the 360°/n formula with n = 24 and then list the first few multiples of 15° to see the pattern.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to also state all 24 angles of symmetry as a complete list and identify which of them are also angles of symmetry for a regular hexagon.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 9.2 p.239
exercise.description: How many lines of symmetry and angles of symmetry does the Ashoka Chakra have?

items.prompt: Which of the following angles can be the smallest angle of rotational symmetry of a figure?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 45°. The smallest angle of rotational symmetry must be a whole-number factor of 360°. 360° ÷ 45° = 8, which is a whole number. The others: 360/17, 360/50, and 360/7 are not whole numbers.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the factor-of-360 criterion: a whole-number angle θ can be the smallest angle of symmetry if and only if 360 ÷ θ is a whole number.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student does not apply the factor test; 360/17 is not a whole number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student does not apply the factor test; 360/50 = 7.2, not a whole number.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student does not apply the factor test; 360/7 is not a whole number.

inclusivity.support: Have the student divide 360 by each option and check whether the result is a whole number.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to list all whole-number angles between 1° and 90° that can be a smallest angle of symmetry.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 9.2 p.238
exercise.description: Can a figure have rotational symmetry whose smallest angle of symmetry is: (a) 45°? (b) 17°?

items.prompt: How many angles of rotational symmetry do the regular polygons have? Write the sequence for the regular triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon, and heptagon (7 sides).

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Regular triangle: 3, regular square: 4, regular pentagon: 5, regular hexagon: 6, regular heptagon: 7. The sequence is 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 — for a regular n-gon, the number of angles of rotational symmetry is n.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: For a regular n-gon, apply the 360°/n formula: there are n distinct multiples of 360°/n from 360°/n up to 360°, giving n angles of symmetry.

inclusivity.support: Have the student use the table of regular-polygon results (Q8 and Q9) to read off the angle count for each polygon.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state the smallest angle of symmetry for each polygon in the sequence and identify the pattern in those smallest angles.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 9.2 p.239
exercise.description: How many angles of symmetry do the Regular Polygons (from Chapter 1, Table 3) have? What number sequence do you get?

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Figures with more than one line of symmetry
items.section_title: Figures with more than one line of symmetry
items.prompt: Explain why the diagonal of a rectangle that is not a square cannot be a line of symmetry. Use the definition of a line of symmetry in your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: When a non-square rectangle is folded along its diagonal, the two triangular halves do not overlap exactly: the longer sides fall on the shorter sides, so corresponding points do not coincide. Since folding along the diagonal does not produce exact overlap of both halves, the diagonal is not a line of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the fold-and-overlap definition: a non-square rectangle's diagonal fold maps a longer side onto a shorter side, so the halves cannot coincide.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to fold a rectangular sheet along the diagonal, observe what happens to the corners, and describe the mismatch before writing the explanation.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if the rectangle were made into a square by trimming, at what point would the diagonal become a line of symmetry, and why?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 9.1 p.221
exercise.description: Is the diagonal of a rectangle (that is not a square) a line of symmetry? Fold a rectangular piece of paper along its diagonal to check whether the two parts overlap.

items.prompt: A shape is made of two identical parallelogram strips placed side by side so that together they form a larger parallelogram shape. Explain, using the definition of rotational symmetry, whether this combined shape has rotational symmetry. In your answer, state what happens when the shape is rotated by 180° about its centre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A parallelogram — including one formed by combining two parallelogram strips — does not have rotational symmetry in the chapter's sense (only 360° returns it to itself). When rotated 180° about its centre, the longer sides of the parallelogram slant in the opposite direction, so the rotated shape does not coincide with the original. Because the 180° rotation changes the orientation of the slanted sides, the only angle of symmetry is 360°. A figure with only 360° as its angle of symmetry does not have rotational symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the definition: a rotation is an angle of symmetry only if the figure looks exactly the same afterward; a 180° rotation of a parallelogram produces an image with the slant in the opposite direction, which does not match.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to trace the combined shape, rotate the tracing 180°, and describe whether it matches the original before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: what modification to the combined parallelogram shape would give it rotational symmetry, and what would the new smallest angle of symmetry be?

exercise.book_ref: Example, section 9.2 p.232
exercise.description: Find the angles of symmetry of a parallelogram-strip shape. A 180° rotation is demonstrated not to overlap with the original (asymmetry of the parallelogram); the figure returns to itself only after 360°, so it does not have rotational symmetry.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: Priya folds a square piece of paper in half vertically and places an ink blot on the right half. She presses the two halves together and opens the paper. Describe the line of symmetry of the resulting ink-blot shape and explain why that line is a line of symmetry.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The resulting ink-blot shape has a vertical line of symmetry running along the fold line — the crease where the paper was folded. It is a line of symmetry because folding the paper along that crease maps the ink mark on the right half exactly onto the mirror copy printed on the left half, so both halves overlap exactly when folded along the vertical crease.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the fold-and-overlap definition: the vertical fold crease is the line of symmetry because folding along it maps each point of the mark to its mirror image produced by pressing.

inclusivity.support: Have the student physically fold and press a piece of paper with a mark, then fold the result along the crease to confirm the overlap before writing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if Priya made two folds — vertical then horizontal — before applying ink and pressing, how many lines of symmetry would the result have and where would they lie?

exercise.book_ref: Activity: Ink Blot Devils, section 9.1 p.222
exercise.description: Students fold paper in half, spill ink on one half, press halves together, and open to observe the symmetric figure formed, identifying the fold as the line of symmetry.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: A square sheet of paper is folded once horizontally (top half folds onto bottom half). A hole is punched through both layers at a point that is 3 cm from the left edge and 2 cm below the fold line. When the paper is unfolded, how many holes are there, and what are their distances from the fold line?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: There are 2 holes. One hole is 2 cm below the fold line (the punched hole on the bottom half). The other hole is 2 cm above the fold line (the mirror hole created on the top half), because folding maps a point 2 cm below the fold onto a point 2 cm above the fold. Both holes are 3 cm from the left edge.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the reflection principle: folding reflects a point at distance d below the fold line to a point at distance d above the fold line; punching through both layers creates one hole on each side at the same distance from the fold.

inclusivity.support: Have the student fold a piece of paper and physically punch a hole, then unfold and measure both holes' distances from the fold crease.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if the paper had been folded twice — first horizontally then vertically — and a single punch were made, how many holes would appear when unfolded and where would they be?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 9.1 p.224
exercise.description: In each of four figures, a hole was punched in a folded square sheet and then unfolded. Identify the fold line. For figure (d), created by a single punch, determine how the paper was folded.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: A square sheet of paper is folded along its vertical midline. A triangular piece is cut from the folded edge. When the paper is opened, describe the shape of the hole and state how many lines of symmetry it has.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Cutting a triangle from the folded edge creates a hole that is a rhombus (or kite, depending on the cut angle) when the paper is opened, because the cut appears symmetrically on both layers. The hole has at least one line of symmetry — the vertical fold line — because folding along it maps the left half of the hole onto the right half exactly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the folding principle: any cut made through both layers of a single vertical fold is reflected across the fold line, producing a hole that is symmetric about that line.

inclusivity.support: Have the student fold and cut paper, open it, and trace the hole before answering — then fold the traced hole along the crease to confirm symmetry.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to predict what shape of hole results if the triangle is cut from the non-folded edge instead of the folded edge, and whether it still has the same line of symmetry.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 9.1 p.224
exercise.description: Paper cutting questions using vertical and horizontal fold notation; interpret representations of folded paper and associated cuts.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: A square piece of paper is folded twice: first along the vertical midline, then along the horizontal midline. A small square piece is cut from the corner where both fold lines meet. How many square holes appear when the paper is fully unfolded, and where are they located?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: One hole appears — at the centre of the original square — because both fold lines meet at the centre of the sheet. When the paper is folded twice, the corner where both fold lines intersect corresponds to the very centre of the full sheet. Cutting from that corner removes a small square from all four layers simultaneously, and when unfolded, a single hole appears at the centre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Track the corner produced by both folds: the intersection of the vertical and horizontal midlines is the centre of the original sheet, so a cut at that corner removes paper from all four layers, producing one hole at the centre.

inclusivity.support: Have the student fold paper twice and mark the corner where both folds meet, then cut and unfold to verify before answering.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if the small square were cut from the outer corner (away from both fold lines) instead, how many holes would appear and where?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 9.1 p.226
exercise.description: Determine how to obtain each of two shapes (both with a square hole in the centre) using folds and a single straight cut — sub-parts (a) aligned-square hole and (b) diamond-orientation square hole.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: Look at a shape made of four identical rhombuses arranged so that they share a common centre point and each rhombus points in a different direction. Does this shape have any lines of symmetry? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The shape depends on the exact orientation of the rhombuses. If the four rhombuses are arranged with equal 90° gaps between them and each is a mirror image of the one opposite, the arrangement has lines of symmetry at 0°, 90° (vertical and horizontal) and possibly the diagonals — up to 4 lines. The student should apply the fold-and-overlap test for each candidate line. A symmetrically arranged four-rhombus figure typically has 4 lines of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the fold-and-overlap definition to each candidate line through the centre: a line is a line of symmetry only if folding maps every rhombus onto an identical rhombus on the other side.

inclusivity.support: Have the student trace the four-rhombus figure and fold along different lines to check overlap physically.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to modify the arrangement so that the shape has exactly 2 lines of symmetry instead of 4, and explain what change achieves this.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q7, section 9.1 p.227
exercise.description: Trace each of eight figures (arrangements of rhombus shapes and polygons on grids) and draw the lines of symmetry, if any.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: Draw a closed figure that contains at least one curved side and has exactly two lines of symmetry. Describe where the two lines of symmetry lie in your figure.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A valid example is a shape like a horizontal oval (ellipse): one line of symmetry runs horizontally through the centre (left-right mirror) and one runs vertically through the centre (top-bottom mirror). Each line divides the figure into two halves that overlap exactly when folded along it. The figure must have no additional lines of symmetry.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the fold-and-overlap definition for each symmetry line; the student must verify that only two directions produce exact overlap.

inclusivity.support: Have the student start with a rectangle (which has two lines of symmetry) and then round its corners to produce a curved figure with the same two lines.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to draw a different example — not an oval — that also has exactly two lines of symmetry and at least one curved side, and verify both lines.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 9.1 p.228
exercise.description: Draw figures containing at least one curved boundary with exactly: (a) one line of symmetry; (b) two lines of symmetry; (c) four lines of symmetry.

items.section_ref: section 9.1 — Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.section_title: Generating shapes having lines of symmetry
items.prompt: On squared paper, a partial figure has its left half drawn. The vertical midline is given as the line of symmetry. One corner of the left half is at the point 3 squares to the left of the midline and 4 squares above the baseline. Where must the corresponding corner of the right half lie? State its position relative to the midline and the baseline.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The corresponding corner must lie 3 squares to the right of the midline and 4 squares above the baseline. Reflecting across the vertical midline maps a point at distance 3 to the left to a point at distance 3 to the right; the vertical distance (4 squares above the baseline) is unchanged.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply reflection across a vertical line: the horizontal distance from the line is preserved in magnitude but switches side; the vertical distance remains the same.

inclusivity.support: Have the student fold the squared paper along the midline and mark the dot, then unfold to see where it lands on the right side.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if the line of symmetry were diagonal (at 45°) instead of vertical, where would the same corner be reflected to? Describe the new position.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 9.1 p.229
exercise.description: Copy six partial drawings on squared paper and complete each so that the resulting figure has both blue lines as lines of symmetry — sub-parts (a) through (f).

items.prompt: A designer creates a logo using a regular octagon (8 equal sides and 8 equal angles). State how many lines of symmetry the logo has and list all its angles of rotational symmetry. Then explain whether the logo has more lines of symmetry than a regular hexagon.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A regular octagon has 8 lines of symmetry and 8 angles of rotational symmetry: 45°, 90°, 135°, 180°, 225°, 270°, 315°, and 360°. A regular hexagon has 6 lines of symmetry, so the octagon has more lines of symmetry than the hexagon (8 > 6).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the regular-polygon rules: a regular n-gon has n lines of symmetry and n angles of symmetry, the smallest being 360°/n; here n = 8 gives smallest angle 45°.

inclusivity.support: Have the student use the completed regular-polygon table (Q8 and Q9) to look up the hexagon's values, then apply the same formula for n = 8.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the smallest regular polygon that has more angles of symmetry than a regular octagon and state its smallest angle of symmetry.
